titulo: The Puzzles of the Centro Storico
intro: You're about to walk over a Roman stadium, in front of a temple that lies about who built it, and right past the exact spot where Julius Caesar was assassinated. Rome doesn't hide its history in museums: it leaves it in the middle of the square, in plain sight of anyone who stops to look. It's about 2 km in total.
puntoPartida: Piazza della Rotonda, facing the Pantheon

paradas.titulo: The building that lies about its own name
paradas.llegada: Stay in Piazza della Rotonda, facing the Pantheon's columns. No need to go in: what you're looking for can be read from the square, on the stone band right above the columns.
paradas.enigma: There, in bronze letters set into the stone, it reads: M·AGRIPPA·L·F·COS·TERTIVM·FECIT — "Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, built this." The building in front of you actually dates from 118-125 AD, built on the orders of Emperor Hadrian almost 150 years after Agrippa died — but Hadrian chose to keep his name on the façade. According to that inscription, how many times had Agrippa been consul?
pistas: Look at the Latin word TERTIVM, the last one before FECIT ("built this").
TERTIVM means the same as "third" in English.
He had been consul three times.
paradas.historia: Hadrian was famous for designing buildings and letting others take the credit. That's why the Pantheon, one of the boldest domes ever built — still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world — carries the name of a man who had been dead for over a century by the time it was finished.
paradas.fuente: Parco archeologico del Colosseo — Pantheon; portico inscription

paradas.titulo: The animal that holds up wisdom
paradas.llegada: Walk around the Pantheon to the left until you reach Piazza della Minerva, right behind it. In the centre stands a small Egyptian obelisk on the back of a white marble animal.
paradas.enigma: It was designed by Bernini in 1667. The base carries a Latin inscription that essentially says it takes a strong mind to bear solid wisdom — represented here by the strongest animal, carrying the obelisk of Egyptian wisdom. What animal is it?
pistas: It's the same animal that, in the fable, never forgets anything.
It has a trunk and tusks.
It's an elephant.
paradas.historia: Romans fondly call it il Pulcin della Minerva ("Minerva's little chick"), though it has nothing to do with a chicken. The obelisk it carries is genuinely Egyptian, from the 6th century BC: Bernini reused a real antiquity for his sculptural joke about the weight of knowledge.

paradas.llegada: Walk to Piazza Navona and stand at its northern end, by the fountain furthest from the domed church.
paradas.enigma: This square is oval-shaped because it's built literally on top of a 1st-century stadium: that of Domitian, where 30,000 spectators once watched athletic contests. The fountain in front of you shows Neptune in the middle of a battle, surrounded by nereids and cherubs. What sea creature is he fighting?
pistas: It has eight arms, not scales or fins.
It's the same animal called polpo in Italian.
Neptune is fighting an octopus.
paradas.historia: This fountain went almost three hundred years without any sculptures: the basin was made by Giacomo della Porta in 1574, but the sculptural group wasn't added until 1878, so as not to compete with Bernini's far more famous central fountain. Beneath the ground you're standing on, the tiers of Domitian's stadium are still there — they can be visited at the Stadio di Domiziano, right underneath the square.
paradas.fuente: Turismo Roma — Fontana del Nettuno; Sovraintendenza Capitolina

paradas.llegada: Walk to the exact centre of the square, where an obelisk rises above four reclining marble figures, one at each corner.
paradas.enigma: This is Bernini's Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi (1651): each figure represents a great river from a continent known at the time — the Nile, the Ganges, the Danube and the Río de la Plata. One of the four has its head covered with a marble cloth. Which river is it — and why do you think it's covered? (you only need the river's name)
pistas: It's the river representing Africa.
In the 17th century, no one in Europe knew where this river's source was.
It's the Nile, veiled because its source was a mystery.
paradas.historia: The source of the Nile wasn't documented until the 19th century, two centuries after Bernini carved this fountain. Look at the obelisk too: it seems to float over a gap in the rock, barely touching its base — an engineering trick Bernini openly bragged about solving.
paradas.fuente: Comune di Roma — Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi

paradas.llegada: Leave the square on the south-west side and find the small Piazza di Pasquino, where a heavily worn marble torso stands on a pedestal.
paradas.enigma: This Roman sculpture, unearthed in 1501, became Rome's anonymous voice: at night, people would stick sheets of paper here with satirical jabs at the Pope and the powerful, knowing no one would be punished for something said "by the statue." Those sheets had their own name, taken from the statue's nickname. Check whether something is still stuck there today — the tradition hasn't quite died. What were those messages called?
pistas: The name comes straight from the statue's nickname: Pasquino.
Add "-ades" to the statue's name.
They were called pasquinades.
paradas.historia: One pope even threatened to have the statue thrown into the Tiber; another, in 1728, sentenced anyone caught posting pasquinades to death. Neither succeeded: Pasquino was Rome's first "free wall," centuries before the phrase free press existed.

paradas.titulo: The four columns of the crime
paradas.llegada: Head south to Largo di Torre Argentina, a sunken square surrounded by a railing: look down, no need to climb in or pay for entry.
paradas.enigma: These ruins are four temples from the Roman Republic, the oldest still standing in the city. Right here, in what was then Pompey's Curia, a group of senators stabbed Julius Caesar 23 times on the Ides of March, 44 BC. Count the temples you can make out among the ruins.
pistas: They're identified by letters, A through D, on the information panels.
There are more than three.
There are four temples.
paradas.historia: The exact spot of Caesar's assassination, according to archaeologists, is marked today by a concrete structure among the ruins. Since the 1990s, the square has also been a cat sanctuary run by volunteers: the cats of Rome unknowingly guard the setting of one of history's most famous conspiracies.
paradas.fuente: Sovraintendenza Capitolina — Area Sacra di Largo Argentina

paradas.llegada: Head west to Piazza Farnese, in front of the grand Renaissance palace (today the French Embassy).
paradas.enigma: The square has two twin fountains made from enormous Egyptian granite tubs that once belonged to the Baths of Caracalla. In 1626, architect Girolamo Rainaldi topped them with the emblem of the family the square is named after. What heraldic flower crowns each of the two fountains?
pistas: It's the same symbol found on the flag of Florence and on the coat of arms of many European monarchies.
In Italian it's called giglio; in French, fleur-de-lis.
It's a lily (fleur-de-lis), the Farnese family's emblem.
paradas.historia: Those granite tubs each weigh several tonnes and travelled from the Baths of Caracalla, across the city, to end up decorating the square of one of the most powerful families of the Roman Renaissance. The Farnese gave the Church a pope, Paul III, and their palace remains, centuries later, a diplomatic seat — now France's.
paradas.fuente: Ambasciata di Francia a Roma — Palazzo Farnese; Wikipedia — Fontane di Piazza Farnese

paradas.llegada: Walk to the neighbouring Campo de' Fiori, the site of the daily market. In its centre, a hooded bronze figure stares fixedly toward the Vatican.
paradas.enigma: This is Giordano Bruno, a philosopher condemned as a heretic and burned alive on this exact spot in 1600 for holding, among other ideas, that the universe was infinite and contained other worlds. The statue was erected almost three centuries later. On the pedestal, beneath his feet, there's a date carved in Roman numerals: IX GIUGNO MDCCCLXXXIX. What year does that correspond to?
pistas: MDCCCLXXXIX breaks down into M (1000) + DCCC (800) + LXXX (80) + IX (9).
It's a 19th-century year, almost 300 years after Bruno's death.
The year is 1889.
paradas.historia: The inscription reads: "To Bruno — the century he foresaw — here where the stake burned." It was erected during a dispute between the Kingdom of Italy and the Papacy, as a monument to freedom of thought in the face of the Inquisition. Every morning except Sunday, the Campo de' Fiori market sets up its fruit and flower stalls around the statue of the man the Church tried to silence forever.
paradas.fuente: Comune di Roma — Monument to Giordano Bruno; Ettore Ferrari, sculptor (1889)

final.texto: From a dome that lies about who built it, to a square that was once a stadium, from a river with no face to the exact spot where Caesar died, to the ashes of a man punished for imagining infinity. Rome doesn't keep its history behind glass: it leaves it in the street, waiting for someone to stop and read it. You just did.
